closed_this_pass.what: bypass/block lists from configuration (SPEC §6.10; PLAN.md: 'Списки bypass/block §6.10 всё ещё захардкожены… и должны приходить из конфигурации')
closed_this_pass.decision_log: implementation-notes.md, section 'Этап 8 — списки bypass/block §6.10 из конфигурации (routing_lists)', including three Deviations

scope_decision.taken: Both §6.10 lists — bypass AND block — became data (netstack.Routing), not only the service-discovery set. PLAN.md's own wording decided this, not the previous HANDOFF's narrower guess.
scope_decision.floor: §5.6's always-allowed exceptions (loopback/RFC1918/link-local, DHCP, NTP) are NOT removable by configuration: resolveRouting merges them into any non-empty config list. Reason: §5.6 promises that without them fail-close breaks the network itself, and that promise has to hold for a bad config too, not only for the fail-close phase. Same reason bypass is still checked before block in classify — a config block list cannot shadow DHCP (TestRoutingBlockCannotOverrideAlwaysAllowed).
scope_decision.not_floor: Service discovery (mDNS 224.0.0.251:5353, SSDP 239.255.255.250:1900) IS removable: §5.6 does not list it, it lives in §6.10 next to 'блокировать нельзя' for Bonjour/AirPrint, and a network with no printers may legitimately refuse to leak multicast.
scope_decision.out_of_scope: User split prefixes: PLAN.md says they belong in routing rules, not in the bypass verdict, because bypass is NAT through the agent's socket, not transparent forwarding. IPv6 was deliberately left alone — it never reaches classify (§6.9, netstack.go parse !ok branch); ipv6_block is its own queue item.

changed_files.what: New file. Rule{Prefix netip.Prefix; Proto uint8; Port uint16} — zero in a field means 'any' (DHCP has no address; 'local network' has no port), destination only, source is not part of any §6.10 rule. Routing{Bypass, Block []Rule}. DefaultRouting() = alwaysBypass() + serviceDiscovery(), plus defaultBlock(). resolveRouting(*Routing) turns nil into the defaults, merges the §5.6 floor into any non-nil config, and is the single place policy routing_lists is read. Exported ProtoTCP/ProtoUDP so config authors outside netstack need not import gvisor.

isBypass(f, rt) and isBlocked(f, rt) are now one-line matchAny calls; classify(f, healthy, rt) takes the lists as a third parameter and stays a pure function. The hardcoded ranges/ports/addresses moved to routing.go as data; addrMDNS/addrSSDP/addrBcast and the port constants stay here and are consumed by routing.go's defaults.

flowTable holds the resolved *Routing (newFlowTable(clk, idle, rt)). Deliberate: the verdict is taken once per flow (§3.4), so a list changing mid-flow would break that contract more quietly than the list change itself.
Config.Routing *Routing — nil means §6.10 defaults. New() calls resolveRouting(cfg.Routing) once and hands the result to newFlowTable.

Config.Routing *netstack.Routing, passed straight into netstack.Config. A one-line pass-through shaped exactly like Config.DNSUpstreams: a configuration value whose empty state means defaults and which cmd/hop does not set yet.

New policy RoutingLists (routing_lists), registered in All() next to NATKey/BypassSink. It gates the reading of the configuration inside resolveRouting: with the policy off the config is ignored entirely and DefaultRouting() is used, i.e. exactly the pre-pass hardcoded behavior. That is why T17 and T31 stay green in both states.
newHarness(t, healthy, opts ...func(*Config)) — variadic Config tweaks so T32 can build a stack with a config-supplied routing table. Existing call sites unchanged.

new_tests.note: The first two and T32 are the registered guards for routing_lists, verified red under HOP_DISABLE=routing_lists (TestRoutingBlockListComesFromConfig reddens too but is left unregistered to keep negcheck's cost down). T32 runs through the fake PacketDevice on a fail-close stand (no live nodes) on purpose: it proves 'the configuration let this flow out to the local network' in its strongest form — against a closed tunnel — and it synchronizes on FakeDevice.WaitEmitted (2 s) via a second packet rather than on fakenet.Bypass.WaitPackets, which waits forever and would make the guard hang instead of redden. Same trick as TestBypassSendErrorCountsAsBlocked.

stayed_green: TestT17MDNSGoesToLocalNetwork (internal/netstack) — green with the policy on and off, by design: it exercises the defaults, and the defaults reproduce the old hardcoded set one for one.
TestBypassMDNSReachesPhysicalInterfaceAndReturnsViaNAT (T31, internal/l3) — re-run under `unshare -Urn`, PASS; the whole internal/l3 suite PASS as well.
deviations: Block list default is 224.0.0.0/4 while SPEC §6.10's text says 224.0.0.0/3. The pre-pass code blocked multicast via netip.Addr.IsMulticast, i.e. exactly 224.0.0.0/4; /3 additionally covers the reserved 240.0.0.0/4, which was never blocked. Widening the block to the spec's letter while turning code into data would have hidden a behavior change inside a refactor, so the default reproduces the old behavior exactly and the divergence is recorded. Anyone wanting the letter adds 240.0.0.0/4 through configuration — which is the point of the list being configurable.

The §5.6 floor is written as IPv4 prefixes (127.0.0.0/8, RFC1918, 169.254.0.0/16), which is not equivalent to the old IsLoopback/IsPrivate/IsLinkLocalUnicast predicates for IPv6 (::1, fc00::/7, fe80::/10). No difference exists today: IPv6 never reaches classify (§6.9). Rule.matches uses netip.Prefix.Contains, false across address families, so an IPv4 list cannot accidentally leak IPv6 once IPv6 does reach the verdict — TestRoutingIPv4RuleDoesNotMatchIPv6 pins that in advance.

'Configuration' currently stops at agent.Config. Neither the CLI nor the store fills the lists — the source is programmatic only, exactly like Config.DNSUpstreams, which cmd/hop also never sets. The on-disk format, the CLI surface and validation of user-supplied prefixes are a §5.9/store question, deliberately not solved in the same pass that turned the list into data. Queued.

next_task.name: RST for TCP-to-LAN instead of a silent drop
next_task.why_first: It is the last place where a verdict lies about what happens to the packet: verdict Bypass is decided for a TCP flow and the packet is then dropped without a word. §5.6's 'закрытие — отказ, а не молчание' is the same rule that already produced internal/reject for Reject and for orphaned; TCP-to-LAN is the one flow still outside it.
current_state: internal/netstack/netstack.go, handle(), case Bypass: the packet goes to s.cfg.Bypass.Send(pkt). internal/bypass/bypass.go returns ErrUnsupported for anything that is not IPv4/UDP, so a TCP SYN to an RFC1918/loopback/link-local address ends as Stats.Blocked and a drop. The application then waits out its connect timeout — the exact failure mode §5.6 calls out.
internal/reject already builds both answers (RST for TCP, ICMP port/host unreachable for UDP) and is used for verdict Reject a few lines below in the same switch; reject.Reply(pkt) is the whole call.

The BypassSink pass's final review (finding 1) named internal/reject as the right answer here and explicitly deferred it. See implementation-notes.md, 'Этап 9 — BypassSink', Deviations ('Только UDP').

Do not confuse this with the drop of an unreachable bypass sink (nil sink / ErrDisabled / socket error): that one is already counted in Stats.Blocked as a deliberate decision of the BypassSink pass. This task is the verdict-level TCP-to-LAN case, refused by internal/bypass rather than delivered.
next_task.goal: A TCP SYN whose verdict is Bypass gets a refusal instead of silence: RST back to the client on the same single-writer path Reject already uses. Decide, and argue in implementation-notes.md, whether UDP that bypass refuses (ErrUnsupported/ErrDisabled/socket error) should also answer ICMP unreachable instead of being a silent Stats.Blocked — the two cases mean different things and the answer should be reasoned, not assumed.
reuse: internal/reject.Reply(pkt) — same function, same call shape as netstack.go's case Reject. It already refuses to answer what it considers a §5.6 exception (reject.Excluded), so check what it does with an RFC1918 destination before assuming it answers at all. internal/netstack/verdict_test.go's TestRejectVerdictNeverEndsInSilence is the existing seam test between those two lists and is the model for the new one.

policy.RejectMode already gates 'refuse instead of drop' for verdict Reject (guards T12/T13). Decide whether TCP-to-LAN belongs under the same flag or needs its own; the argument matters more than the answer, since RejectMode's doc frames it as fail-close and this is not fail-close.
netstack.Routing (this pass) is unaffected: membership in the bypass list is decided before handle() ever looks at the protocol.

Per-task gate only needs the new policy's own guard under HOP_DISABLE=<name>, not a full negcheck run — the controller runs the full one at the end of the pass.
notes.realtimelint: does not accept ./... as an argument — pass literally `.`
notes.l3_how_to_run: Build once, run under an unprivileged user namespace: `go test -c -o /tmp/l3.test ./internal/l3` then `HOP_L3=1 unshare -Urn /tmp/l3.test` (add `-test.v -test.run '<pattern>'` to scope it). This works without root — unshare -Urn grants CAP_NET_ADMIN inside the fresh netns. Building the test binary once and reusing it across repeated unshare invocations is much faster than `go test` per run when iterating.

queue_after_routing_lists.task: Invalidate bypass sockets on interface change
queue_after_routing_lists.detail: bypass.NAT binds each socket to Selector.Interface() at creation (internal/bypass/bypass.go:143) and never re-binds it; nothing ties the NAT's socket cache to outbound.Selector's interface-change signal. Worse, socket.seen is refreshed on every Send (bypass.go:139), not only on a successful round trip, so periodic service-discovery retries (mDNS/SSDP) keep a dead-bound socket alive past the Idle sweep indefinitely. See implementation-notes.md Deviations (Этап 9) for the full writeup and §6.8's 'следствие первое'.
shapes: NAT.Reset() called by outbound.Selector's rtnetlink watcher on interface change (close all sockets; next Send re-dials)
a hard TTL on socket age independent of seen, so a socket dies by age even under continuous traffic
queue_after_routing_lists.why_deferred: properly wiring either shape touches outbound.Selector's rtnetlink watcher, which is outside BypassSink's scope (Global Constraint 9, constraints.md).

queue_after_routing_lists.detail: bypass.NAT.Stats() (internal/bypass/bypass.go:227) is unreachable in production today — nothing outside internal/bypass/bypass_test.go calls it, and Stack.Stats() (internal/netstack/netstack.go) does not fold it in the way it folds in natTable's stats. In production the idle sweep of bypass sockets therefore only runs on Send, and persists until Down after traffic stops — parity with natTable, not a regression, but Stats() staying unreachable means bypass socket/goroutine counts are invisible to whatever eventually surfaces Stack.Stats (CLI status, metrics).
queue_after_routing_lists.note: final review (finding 9) fixed only the Stats() doc comment to say this plainly; the architecture (wiring it into Stack.Stats) is this queue item, not done in that pass.
